opus-5.5.text:
I think what Jitendra means is that the problems in robotics are too fundamental to stay inside one narrow community. For a long time, robotics was driven by people trained in control theory, kinematics, and very careful hand-engineered pipelines. That tradition achieved a lot, but it also built a culture: you model the system precisely, design a controller, and verify it in a well-defined setting. That works well in a factory. It works much less well in an open, messy world.

For robot foundation models, I read the statement this way: the breakthroughs we need probably won't come only from better motor controllers or better grippers. They'll come from bringing in ideas from computer vision, from language modeling, from large-scale machine learning, and even from cognitive science and developmental psychology. Jitendra has always pushed this. He came from vision, and he often reminds us that perception, action, and learning can't really be separated. Babies don't learn to grasp from a physics model. They learn through huge amounts of embodied experience.

What we've seen in the last few years supports this. Many of the important shifts in robot learning came from people who brought a "scale and data" mindset from vision and NLP: using pretrained vision-language backbones, treating actions almost like tokens, and caring more about data diversity than about perfecting a single task. Many people with traditional robotics training were initially skeptical, and for understandable reasons. The skepticism was healthy, but it couldn't be the only voice.

I don't read it as dismissive of roboticists, though. The other half is just as important. People from machine learning often underestimate how hard the physical world is: contact, latency, hardware failures, safety, the fact that you can't simply scrape a trillion tokens of robot data from the internet. Building a foundation model for robots needs people who have actually fought with real hardware at 2 a.m. So for me the message is about mixing cultures. The field needs the ambition and scaling intuition of the AI community combined with the physical grounding and rigor of roboticists.

There's also a broader point. If robots really become general-purpose, they'll affect labor, homes, elder care, and manufacturing, so the questions become societal, not just technical. That's another sense in which robotics is too important to be left only to roboticists.

r001.rationale: The candidate says robotics needs ideas and contributions beyond a narrow community, but explicitly frames the quote as not dismissive of roboticists and calls for combining their expertise with AI. It does not clearly suggest outsiders must intervene because robotics specialists cannot deliver the field’s promise.

r002.rationale: The candidate clearly calls for combining robotics with computer vision, language modeling, machine learning, and other disciplines. It mentions industries such as manufacturing and elder care as areas robots may affect, but does not clearly say development requires collaboration across industries.

fable-5.1.text:
I think Jitendra was being deliberately provocative, but there's a real point underneath it. The way I read it, it's a riff on the old line that war is too important to be left to the generals. He's saying that the robotics community, for a long time, treated the problem as primarily a hardware and controls problem. Better actuators, better kinematics, better trajectory optimization. All of that matters, but it turned out the biggest unlock in the last few years didn't come from inside robotics at all. It came from people working on language models and vision models who had never touched a robot.

So when we talk about robot foundation models, I think his statement is really about where the ideas have to come from. The things that made large models work in language, scaling laws, pretraining on internet-scale data, learning representations that transfer, these were developed by people who weren't thinking about grasping or locomotion. And when roboticists first encountered them, there was a lot of resistance. People said the real world is different, you can't just throw data at it, the physics won't let you. Some of that skepticism was correct. But a lot of it was the field protecting its own intuitions.

Where I'd push back a little is that I don't think he means roboticists should step aside. I think he means the opposite, that the field has to open up. Robotics is going to be the place where all of AI actually lands in the physical world, and that's too big a thing for one community to own. You need people who understand data at scale, people who understand how to build evaluation that doesn't lie to you, people who understand vision and language, and yes, people who understand how a gripper actually behaves when it closes on a wet cup.

The part I take most seriously is the humility piece. In my own work, the moments where we made the most progress were usually when someone outside the robotics tradition asked a naive question. Why do you collect data this way? Why is the action space so hand-designed? Why do you evaluate on ten episodes? And the honest answer was often "because that's how it's always been done." Foundation models force you to confront those habits, because the recipe only works if you're willing to let the data and the model tell you things you didn't expect.

So I'd interpret the statement as a call to treat robotics as a shared frontier rather than a guild. The robotists, to use his word, still have essential knowledge. But if we want models that generalize across tasks and embodiments, that knowledge has to be combined with ideas from people who've already watched scaling work once, and who aren't attached to the assumptions that held the field back.

r001.rationale: The candidate acknowledges that ideas from outside robotics helped advance the field, but rejects the idea that roboticists should step aside and calls their knowledge essential. It does not offer the specified less charitable interpretation that outsiders must intervene because robotics specialists cannot deliver the field’s promise.

r002.rationale: The candidate says robot foundation models require combining robotics expertise with contributions from people working in data, evaluation, vision, and language, describing robotics as a shared frontier.

astra-6.text:
I interpret that as a call to broaden who contributes to robotics. If we want robots to operate in the real world, building the robot is only part of the problem. We also need learning, perception, reasoning, and an understanding of what people actually need robots to do.

That becomes especially relevant with robot foundation models. Robotics expertise is essential because physical interaction introduces constraints that you can’t ignore: safety, timing, hardware limitations, and the consequences of an action. But we also need contributions from people working on large-scale learning, data, and general-purpose models, as well as people who understand the environments where robots will be used.

So I wouldn’t read the statement as dismissing roboticists. I’d read it as saying that robotics is too consequential to remain within one discipline. The opportunity is to bring those communities together, while keeping the models grounded in what actually works in the physical world.

r001.rationale: The response frames the quote as broadening participation and explicitly says it is not dismissing roboticists; it does not suggest outsiders must intervene because specialists cannot deliver robotics’ promise.

r002.rationale: The response calls for bringing different communities together and names several disciplines, but it does not clearly communicate collaboration across industries.

sol-6.1.text:
I interpret that as a call to broaden who gets to shape robotics. With robot foundation models, you’re not just solving a control problem. You’re bringing together learning, perception, language, hardware, and an understanding of what people actually need a robot to do.

Roboticists bring essential expertise: the physical world is unforgiving, and a model that looks impressive in a demonstration may still fail when the environment changes. But progress also needs people who understand how to train general models, build useful data infrastructure, and design interactions that people can trust.

So, to me, the statement isn’t dismissing roboticists. It’s saying the ambition is bigger than any one discipline. And the test of a robot foundation model shouldn’t just be how many tasks it can demonstrate in a lab. It should be whether it can reliably help people in real settings, and whether the people using it have a voice in its development.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly says the quote is not dismissing roboticists and frames it as broadening participation, not as saying specialists cannot deliver robotics’ promise.

r002.rationale: It says progress requires bringing together learning, perception, language, hardware, model training, data infrastructure, and interaction design, clearly expressing cross-disciplinary collaboration.
